titulo_es: Ellipsis and substitution (so, not, do so, one/ones)
descripcion_es: Avoiding repetition with so, not, do so, one/ones, auxiliaries on their own and to without a verb.
resumen: English avoids repeating words by leaving them out (ellipsis) or replacing them with short words such as so, not, one, do so. Unlike Spanish, it almost never leaves a clause without something to “support” it: an auxiliary, to, so or one.

filas: I don't like the red shirt; I prefer the blue one.
A clause, after think, hope, expect, suppose, believe, be afraid
Will it rain? I think so.
A negative clause, after hope, be afraid, suppose, guess
Is he coming? I hope not.
do so / do it / do that
He promised to help, and he did so immediately.
She can swim, but I can't.
I didn't want to go, but I had to.
I'm tired. So am I. / I don't smoke. Neither do I.

items: With think, believe, expect and suppose, the most natural negative is I don't think so; I think not is formal. With hope and be afraid only I hope not / I'm afraid not is possible.
One is not used with uncountable nouns: I like white wine more than red (not “red one”).
Do so is more formal than do it; it is common in written texts and presentations.
The repeated auxiliary agrees in tense: He has finished, and so have I.

explicacion.texto: Spanish speakers tend to copy Spanish “creo que sí” as “I think yes” or “I think that yes”, and to leave the clause without support: “I wanted to go but I couldn't go it”. The correct forms are I think so and I wanted to, but I couldn't.

ejemplos.frase: Are you coming to the party? I'm afraid not.
ejemplos.traduccion: ¿Vienes a la fiesta? Me temo que no.

ejemplos.frase: These boots are too small; I need bigger ones.
ejemplos.traduccion: Estas botas me quedan pequeñas; necesito unas más grandes.

ejemplos.frase: The board was asked to reconsider, but it declined to do so.
ejemplos.traduccion: Se pidió al consejo que lo reconsiderara, pero se negó a hacerlo.

ejemplos.frase: I'd love to visit Japan one day. Who wouldn't?
ejemplos.traduccion: Me encantaría visitar Japón algún día. ¿A quién no?

ejemplos.frase: You don't have to come if you don't want to.
ejemplos.traduccion: No tienes que venir si no quieres.

ejemplos.frase: My sister has never been to Canada, and neither have I.
ejemplos.traduccion: Mi hermana nunca ha estado en Canadá, y yo tampoco.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Is the shop open? I think yes.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Is the shop open? I think so.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Spanish “creo que sí” is I think so.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I wanted to call you, but I couldn't do.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I wanted to call you, but I couldn't.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The modal is enough to replace the verb; do is not added.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Do you want to come with us? Yes, I want.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Do you want to come with us? Yes, I want to.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Want needs the support of to when the infinitive is left out; in Spanish “sí, quiero” is enough.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: He has a big car and a small.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: He has a big car and a small one.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: An adjective with an article cannot stand alone: one is needed.

ejercicios.frase: Will the meeting be cancelled? I hope ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the Rules and key points table that not replaces a negative clause after hope, be afraid, suppose or guess. The clue is the verb hope and the meaning of the answer: the speaker wants the meeting not to be cancelled, that is, not replaces “the meeting won't be cancelled”. With hope the negative is not made with don't (I don't hope so is not used) but by adding not at the end: I hope not. It is the only correct answer.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With hope, the negative answer is I hope not.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Se cancelará la reunión? Espero que no.

por_opcion.not: Correct: I hope not means you hope something will not happen and replaces the whole negative clause.
por_opcion.no: Incorrect: no is a stand-alone answer or a determiner (no money), but it does not replace clauses; “I hope no” is a calque of Spanish “espero que no”.
por_opcion.don't: Incorrect: don't needs a verb after it and there is none here; also, with hope the negative is not made with the auxiliary.
por_opcion.not so: Incorrect: “not so” means “not as” or is used in replies such as “Not so!” (That's not true!), but not after hope.

ejercicios.frase: Is the museum open on Mondays? I don't think ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule in Rules and key points that with think, believe, expect and suppose the most natural negative is I don't think so: the negative moves to the opinion verb and so replaces the clause. The clue is that think is already negative (don't think), so all that is missing is the substitute for “the museum is open on Mondays”, which is so. “I think not” exists, but it is formal and there is already don't here, so the only possible option is so.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The natural form is I don't think so.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Abre el museo los lunes? Creo que no.

por_opcion.it: Incorrect: it replaces a noun, not a clause; “I don't think it” makes no sense in English.
por_opcion.so: Correct: I don't think so is the natural negative answer after think.
por_opcion.not: Incorrect: it would give “I don't think not”, a double negative that would mean the opposite; the formal form would be I think not, without don't.
por_opcion.yes: Incorrect: “I don't think yes” is a calque from Spanish; yes does not replace clauses.

ejercicios.frase: I've lost my umbrella, so I'll have to buy a new ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the first row of the Rules and key points table: one replaces a singular countable noun already mentioned. The clue is umbrella, countable and singular, and the article a before the adjective new: an adjective with an article cannot stand alone, it needs one after it (a new one). Ones would be for a plural, and it would refer to the same lost umbrella, not a new one.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: One replaces a singular countable noun.
ejercicios.traduccion: He perdido el paraguas, así que tendré que comprarme uno nuevo.

por_opcion.it: Incorrect: it refers to the same object already mentioned (the lost umbrella), and also it cannot go after “a new”.
por_opcion.one: Correct: a new one; one replaces umbrella, which is countable and singular.
por_opcion.ones: Incorrect: ones replaces a plural (the red ones) and cannot go with the article a.
por_opcion.some: Incorrect: some is used with plurals or uncountable nouns (I need some new ones / some new paper) and cannot have a before it.

ejercicios.frase: Members may vote by post if they wish to ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: The rule is the one in Rules and key points that do so replaces a predicate (a verb with its complements) and is more formal than do it. The clue is the register: it is a regulatory text (members may vote by post), typical of statutes or rules. Do so replaces “vote by post” and avoids repeating it. In an informal register you would also say “if they wish” or “if they want to”, but among the options only do so is correct.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Do so replaces a predicate in a formal register.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los miembros pueden votar por correo si así lo desean.

por_opcion.do: Incorrect: do on its own after wish to is left hanging; in English the substitute for a predicate is do so, do it or do that, not do alone.
por_opcion.do so: Correct: do so replaces “vote by post” and fits the formal register of the text.
por_opcion.make it: Incorrect: make it means “succeed” or “arrive in time” (I can't make it tonight) and does not replace another verb.
por_opcion.so: Incorrect: so replaces clauses after opinion verbs (I think so), not an infinitive after wish to.

ejercicios.frase: I haven't read the report yet, and neither ___ my colleagues.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row “so / neither + auxiliary + subject” in the table and the rule that the repeated auxiliary agrees in tense. The clue is the verb in the first part, haven't read, in the present perfect: the auxiliary is have. After neither the order is inverted (auxiliary before the subject) and the auxiliary agrees with the plural subject my colleagues, so the result is neither have my colleagues.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Neither + auxiliary in the same tense (have) + subject.
ejercicios.traduccion: Todavía no he leído el informe, y mis compañeros tampoco.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Do is the present simple auxiliary; here the tense is the present perfect (haven't read), so the auxiliary must be have.
Neither is already negative; adding haven't would create a double negative. After neither the auxiliary is affirmative.
The subject is plural (my colleagues), so the auxiliary is have, not has.

ejercicios.frase: She plays the piano much better than I ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule of the auxiliary on its own, which replaces the verb and its complements. The clue is plays, present simple: the auxiliary that stands for it is do (than I do = than I play the piano). Can is also accepted, because “than I can” is grammatical and means “better than I am able to play”, with a nuance of ability. Ending the sentence with “than I” is possible in speech (than me), but the gap asks for an auxiliary.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In the present simple the verb is replaced by do.
ejercicios.traduccion: Ella toca el piano mucho mejor que yo.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Repeating the main verb without its complement sounds incomplete; English uses the auxiliary do to replace it.
Does is for the third person; with the subject I the auxiliary is do.
Am is the verb be, which does not appear in the first part; the auxiliary must correspond to plays, that is, do.

ejercicios.frase: I'd help you if I could, but I'm not allowed ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule “to (without a verb)”: to replaces an infinitive already mentioned. The clue is be allowed, which always takes to + infinitive (allowed to help you); as help you is already in the sentence, to is enough. Spanish says “no me dejan” with nothing more, but in English the sentence cannot end in allowed: it needs the support of to.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: To on its own replaces the infinitive already mentioned.
ejercicios.traduccion: Te ayudaría si pudiera, pero no me está permitido.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “I'm not allowed it” is a calque; after allowed the action is not replaced with it, but with to.
Allowed takes to + infinitive; do without to is not possible here (“allowed to do it” would be, but the gap is for one word).
So replaces clauses after opinion verbs (I think so), not an infinitive after allowed.

ejercicios.frase: Which apples do you want, the green ones or the red ___?
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the one/ones rule in the table: ones replaces a plural countable noun already mentioned. The clue is apples, plural, and the parallel with “the green ones”, which already appears in the same sentence. As red is an adjective with an article (the red), it cannot stand alone as in Spanish (“las rojas”); it needs ones.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Ones replaces a plural countable noun.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Qué manzanas quieres, las verdes o las rojas?

errores_previstos.explicacion: One replaces a singular; apples is plural, so ones is needed.
Repeating the noun is what we want to avoid and, in addition, it should be plural; the correct substitute is ones.
Them is a personal pronoun and cannot go after an article and an adjective (the red them does not exist).

ejercicios.frase: My brother loves horror films, and ___ does my father.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row “so / neither + auxiliary + subject”: to agree with an affirmative statement you use so + auxiliary + subject. The clue is loves (affirmative, present simple) and the auxiliary does, which already appears after the gap. The inverted order (so does my father) is compulsory; Spanish says “y mi padre también”, but in English “and my father too” would be informal and does not fit with does.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: So + auxiliary + subject to agree with an affirmative statement.
ejercicios.traduccion: A mi hermano le encantan las películas de terror, y a mi padre también.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “And also does my father” is not grammatical; the structure for agreeing is so + auxiliary + subject.
Neither is used to agree with a negative statement; loves is affirmative, so so is required.
Too goes at the end (my father does too), not before the auxiliary.

ejercicios.frase: Is it going to snow tomorrow? I'm afraid yes.
respuestas: Is it going to snow tomorrow? I'm afraid so.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule in the table that so replaces an affirmative clause after think, hope, expect, suppose, believe and be afraid. The clue is I'm afraid followed by an affirmative answer (Spanish “que sí”): so replaces “it is going to snow tomorrow”. Yes cannot replace clauses in English; “I'm afraid yes” is a direct calque from Spanish.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “me temo que sí” is I'm afraid so.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Va a nevar mañana? Me temo que sí.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Is it going to snow tomorrow? I'm afraid yes.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: yes does not replace clauses after be afraid; the correct form is I'm afraid so.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Is it going to snow tomorrow? I'm afraid that yes.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of Spanish “me temo que sí”; adding that does not fix it. After be afraid the affirmative substitute is so.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Is it going to snow tomorrow? I'm afraid not.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Not is the negative substitute and changes the meaning to “I'm afraid it won't”; the mistake in the sentence is corrected with so.

ejercicios.frase: I prefer still water to sparkling one.
respuestas: I prefer still water to sparkling.
I prefer still water to sparkling water.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in Rules and key points: one is not used with uncountable nouns. The clue is water, an uncountable noun, so “sparkling one” is not possible. The solution is pure ellipsis (to sparkling) or repeating the noun (to sparkling water); both versions are correct, the first more natural.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: One does not replace uncountable nouns such as water.
ejercicios.traduccion: Prefiero el agua sin gas a la (agua) con gas.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I prefer still water to sparkling one.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: one only replaces countable nouns and water is uncountable.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I prefer still water to sparkling ones.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Ones is also for countable nouns (in the plural); water is still uncountable.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I prefer still water than sparkling.
errores_previstos.explicacion: One has been removed, but to has been changed to than: prefer A to B takes to.

ejercicios.frase: Do you like jazz? Yes, I like.
respuestas: Do you like jazz? Yes, I do.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule of the auxiliary on its own: in short answers the auxiliary replaces the verb with its complement. The clue is the question with do (Do you like jazz?), which is answered with the same auxiliary: Yes, I do. Like is transitive and cannot be left without an object, so “Yes, I like” is a calque of Spanish “sí, me gusta”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The short answer uses the auxiliary do, not the verb like without an object.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Te gusta el jazz? Sí, me gusta.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Do you like jazz? Yes, I like.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: like cannot be left without a complement; the short answer uses the auxiliary do.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Do you like jazz? Yes, I like it.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It is grammatical, but it is not the short answer the substitution exercise asks for; the natural and accepted form is Yes, I do.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Do you like jazz? Yes, I do like.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Do like without an object still leaves like hanging; either say Yes, I do, or Yes, I do like it.

respuestas: I can't come tonight but Sarah can
Sarah can come tonight but I can't
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the rule of the auxiliary on its own: the modal can replaces “come tonight”. The clue is the contrast between two subjects with but: the first part has the full verb (I can't come tonight) and the second only the modal (Sarah can). Spanish says “Sarah sí”, but in English the modal is compulsory. The reverse order is also accepted, Sarah can come tonight but I can't: then the full verb goes in the first part and only the negative auxiliary, can't, in the second.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The auxiliary on its own (can / can't) replaces come tonight.
ejercicios.traduccion: Yo no puedo ir esta noche, pero Sarah sí.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I can't come but Sarah can tonight
errores_previstos.explicacion: Tonight belongs to the first part; placed at the end, it is separated from come and the sentence sounds forced.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Sarah can but I can't come tonight
errores_previstos.explicacion: Here the auxiliary on its own appears before the verb it replaces has been said; in English ellipsis normally refers back to something already mentioned, so the full verb comes first.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I can't come tonight but can Sarah
errores_previstos.explicacion: Inversion with the auxiliary on its own happens with so and neither; in a contrast with but the order is subject + auxiliary.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table: so replaces an affirmative clause after suppose. The order is the normal clause order: subject (I), opinion verb (suppose) and the substitute so at the end. It is the equivalent of Spanish “supongo que sí”; in the negative it would be I don't suppose so or I suppose not.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: So replaces the affirmative clause after suppose.

errores_previstos.explicacion: So at the beginning works as a connector (“so I suppose”), not as a substitute for the clause; the substitute goes after the verb.
So cannot go between the subject and the verb; its place is at the end: I suppose so.

descripcion_larga_es: Ellipsis and substitution let you avoid repeating what has already been said: English does it with short words such as so, not, one, do so, an auxiliary on its own or to without a verb. It is essential for sounding natural in a conversation or a debate, and it is hard for Spanish speakers because Spanish leaves things out without leaving any support (“creo que sí”, “sí, quiero”), while English almost always needs some.

contexto.que_es: Ellipsis means leaving out words that the listener can recover from the context, and substitution means replacing them with a short form. In English the basic tools are one/ones for countable nouns, so and not for whole clauses, do so for predicates, the auxiliary on its own for the verb with its complements and to for an infinitive already mentioned.
contexto.por_que_importa: It is one of the features that most clearly distinguishes natural English from translated English: short answers, agreeing with someone or conceding a point depend on these forms. If you copy Spanish (“I think yes”, “Yes, I like”) the message is understood, but it sounds clearly foreign, and in an oral exam it reveals a level below C1. In written presentations, do so and ellipsis avoid heavy repetition.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: It appears when answering yes/no questions, when giving an opinion with think, hope, suppose or be afraid, when agreeing with another speaker (so do I, neither have I) and when contrasting two subjects (I can't, but she can). The signal is that something has already been said and should not be repeated. Where Spanish leaves the sentence with nothing (“sí, quiero”, “me temo que sí”), English requires support: Yes, I want to; I'm afraid so.
